analysis.one_liner: Bans cash bail in federal criminal cases and cuts grants to states that keep it.
analysis.headline: The bill to end cash bail never received a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for federal judges to require defendants to pay money as a condition of release before trial. It would also make states lose their Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funding if they keep money bail systems, with those funds redistributed to states that switch to non-cash pretrial release. The stated goal is to end a system in which people with money go free before trial while poor people sit in jail, sometimes for months, before any conviction.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income defendants awaiting trial. Under cash bail, people who cannot afford to pay stay in jail before any conviction — the bill's findings say nearly 60 percent of jail inmates are pretrial detainees, an estimated 75 percent charged with nonviolent crimes, and that pretrial detention costs state and local governments an estimated $14 billion a year. Taxpayers also gain if the bill's premise holds, since replacing cash bail with risk-based release decisions could cut those detention costs.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal judge from using payment of money as a condition of pretrial release in criminal cases [S3].
Makes states that use money bail ineligible for Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds beginning the third fiscal year after enactment, with those funds redistributed among eligible states [S3].

The bill's findings state that throughout the nation, people with money can buy their freedom while poor defendants remain incarcerated awaiting trial, and that pretrial detention should turn on risk of not appearing in court or danger to public safety rather than ability to pay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments that keep cash bail would lose federal criminal justice grant money, and the bail bond industry would lose the federal pressure to replace cash bail with non-monetary release. Jurisdictions would also need to build new pretrial assessment systems, which carries a transition cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bail bond industry and states with cash bail

drawbacks.text: The grant penalty hits state budgets and criminal justice programs — drug treatment, crime prevention, victim services — rather than the bail industry itself, so a state could face a punishing funding cut before its legislature agrees to change its bail laws [S3].

Eliminating money bail entirely removes one tool judges can use to encourage court appearance and public safety; opponents of cash bail reform have argued that risk-assessment alternatives can also miss dangerous defendants, and the bill's own findings cite a study showing nearly 50 percent of the most dangerous pretrial detainees are released without supervision under current systems [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending the practice of jailing people before conviction because they cannot pay — is substantial for low-income defendants and follows the principle that detention should depend on risk, not wealth. The main costs fall on states through the grant penalty and on the practical difficulty of replacing cash bail with reliable risk-based release decisions. A fair reading is that the bill's goal is widely shared but its enforcement mechanism (cutting Byrne grants from states) is blunt and would need careful implementation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on September 24, 2019 and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1].
On October 28, 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security; no further action appears in the record [S5].
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Congress ended January 3, 2021 without the bill receiving a hearing or a vote, so it died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income defendants gain nothing because the bill never advanced; the bail bond industry and cash-bail states are better off because the federal grant penalty never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bail bond industry and cash-bail states

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it referred to the Crime subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only four House Democrats ever signed on and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no meaningful partisan breakdown; the outcome reflects inaction rather than opposition on the floor.

industries.note: The bill's central aim is to eliminate payment of money as a condition of pretrial release, which is the bail bond industry's product. By making states without money-bail systems eligible for federal grants and money-bail states ineligible, it pressures the system that keeps the industry in business. The industry profits from the current arrangement, in which defendants who cannot pay remain jailed while paying customers are released.

industries.industry: State and local criminal justice programs (Byrne JAG grantees)
industries.note: States that abolish money bail would keep full grant eligibility, while states that keep it would lose Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds, which support drug treatment, crime prevention, and victim services. The penalty would pressure legislatures to change bail laws but could also cut funding for programs that serve the public.
